root.note: House is a very old Germanic word. Its link to a root meaning ‘to cover’ is only a guess: Etymonline says “perhaps”, and Wiktionary calls the further origin uncertain.

history: House is one of the oldest words in English. In Old English it was hūs, said with a long u, like ‘hoose’. Between about 1400 and 1700 the long vowels of English moved (the Great Vowel Shift), and hūs became house, just as mūs became mouse and lūs became louse. The same old word lives on in German Haus, Dutch huis and Swedish hus. From early on, a house also meant the people in it: the family, and later a royal or noble family, as in the House of Windsor. Parliament has houses too: the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Where the Germanic word comes from is not certain. It may be connected with a root meaning ‘to cover’, but this is only a guess.
historyEinfach: House is a very old English word. A long time ago, people said hūs. It sounded like ‘hoose’. Later the sound changed, and hūs became house. Mouse changed in the same way. In German the word is Haus. In Dutch it is huis. A house is a building. But it can also be a family, like a royal family. Where does the word come from? We don't know for sure. Maybe it means ‘something that covers you’.

synonyms.note: the place where you live and feel you belong
a small house, often in the country
a house with only one floor; from Hindi bangla

cognates.note: ‘town hall’, from German Rathaus through Polish ratusz

elsewhere.text: German Haus and English house are sisters. Both had a long u, and in both languages it later became a diphthong: au in German, ou in English. German Maus and Laus changed in the same way as mouse and louse.

The Germanic house also lives in Russian. Ратуша, the old town hall of a city, comes from German Rathaus, ‘council house’, which travelled east through Polish ratusz. The -hūs part is a cousin of English house.
